newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain in crisis as "dirty war" scandal re-ignited.
newsitem.headline: Spain in crisis as "dirty war" scandal re-ignited.

text.p: Spain plunged into crisis again on Tuesday when opposition parties demanded the resignation of Deputy Prime Minister Francisco Alvarez Cascos after he blamed the former prime minister for a 1980s "dirty war" against Basque guerrillas.
"He should summarily resign," Socialist spokesman Luis Yanez said, adding that Cascos should be locked up "at least in preventive prison" until court proceedings on the dirty war were finished.

Cascos, number two in the ruling Popular Party (PP), set off a political row at the weekend when he accused Socialist former prime minister Felipe Gonzalez of organising a 1983-87 campaign of kidnapping, torture and murder against Basque separatists.
The deputy prime minister said Gonzalez had promoted "wine-cellar terrorism", alluding to a bar in the prime minister's residence where close friends were entertained.

Gonzalez, who said last week that state terrorism never existed during his 13-year rule, has always denied any knowledge of the activities of the GAL (Anti-Terrorist Liberation Groups) which killed 27 suspected guerrillas in the dirty war.
His first interior minister and several high officials in the security forces are on trial on charges that they designed and financed the GAL campaign.
"Mr Gonzalez shows a lot of moral cowardice by shamelessly pawning off the political responsibilities on his subordinates," Cascos said.

The conservative PP government of Jose Maria Aznar has tried to sweep this dark period of Spain's recent history under the carpet and, like the Socialists before it, steadfastly refused to bow to court pressure to hand over classified military intelligence files on the dirty war.
The comment by Cascos is the first sign the party may be changing tactics.

The newspaper El Mundo, quoting PP officials, said the party was worried that the Spanish public was beginning to associate the conservatives with the GAL and Cascos had been used to issue a "warning" to the opposition.
Several opposition parties have accused the PP, which came to power after a "clean hands" campaign, of forming a secret pact with the Socialists to cover up the past.
But it was not clear why Yanez said Cascos should be placed in prison.

The United Left oppoosition coalition called on Tuesday not only for Cascos to resign but also for him to appear in court to testify on any evidence he had for saying Gonzalez was responsible for the dirty war.

Interior Minister Jaime Mayor Oreja told a radio interviewer on Tuesday that the government's policy of leaving the GAL case for the courts to resolve had not changed, but he did not completely disavow the remarks by Cascos.

"Within a government there can be different positions with respect to political responsibilities," he said. "The government as such does not go further at this time than take the position simply that it is the courts that speak."
The political row was reminiscent of the exchange of accusations and counter-accusations that led to the crisis which forced the Socialists to call the last general election.
Spain's Catalan nationalist powerbrokers, who backed the minority Socialist government and now do the same for the PP, warned against further comments that could worsen the political climate.
"We all have a lot to lose," a Catalan coalition official said.
